title: TikTok and YouTube Videos on Overactive Bladder Exhibit Poor Quality and Diversity
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of 136 TikTok and 75 YouTube videos on overactive bladder that reports the share of videos scoring high on a 5-point misinformation scale referenced to clinical guidelines (TikTok 23%/22.8%, YouTube 11%/10.6%). Guideline-discordant content coded explicitly as misinformation and reported as a share of items = CONTENT. The DISCERN 'poor quality' shares are also reported and are kept as QUALITY rows (excluded from prevalence).

estimates.country: not stated (English-language videos only; U.S. author team, U.S. condition prevalence discussed)
estimates.date: searched 13 February 2022 (TikTok API, last 500 videos with #overactivebladder)
estimates.measure_type: % of TikTok videos on overactive bladder rated high or extreme misinformation (score >3 on a 5-point scale referenced to clinical guidelines)
estimates.value_raw: Table 2 'High misinformation (score 3)': 22.8 (34,751); abstract and Discussion text: "Twenty-three percent of TikTok ... had high misinformation (score >3)"; the Results section instead says "Nine percent of TikTok videos"
estimates.denominator: 136 TikTok videos meeting inclusion criteria, drawn from the last 500 videos carrying #overactivebladder (excluding off-topic, non-English, >10-minute, text-and-audio-free and provider-only surgical-technique videos)
estimates.definition: the video scored above 3 (i.e. 4 = high or 5 = extreme misinformation) on a published 5-point misinformation Likert scale rated against clinical guidelines
estimates.misinfo_def: "Misinformation was categorized on a published 5-point Likert scale compared to clinical guidelines (ie, 1¼no misinformation, 2¼very little misinformation, 3¼moderate information, 4¼high misinformation, 5¼extreme misinformation)."

estimates.ground_truth_detail: Trained reviewers scored each video against clinical guidelines after the research team achieved consensus ratings on 6 YouTube and 6 TikTok videos. No reliability statistic is computed for this study; the paper cites a prior study with the same instruments where "interrater reliability was 99.6% between 2 coders". The authors concede "the PEMAT and DISCERN tools have a degree of subjectivity".

estimates.notes: JUDGEMENT CALL - the paper contradicts itself on this value. The abstract and the Table 2 row say 23% / 22.8%, but the Results text says "Nine percent of TikTok videos and 11% of YouTube videos scored high on misinformation (a score >3)." I entered 22.8% because two independent statements (abstract and Table 2) agree, because Table 2's other percentages are all exact fractions of 136 and 75 (87.5% = 119/136, 38.2% = 52/136, 97.8% = 133/136, 60% = 45/75, 26.7% = 20/75, 65.3% = 49/75, 10.6% = 8/75), and 22.8% = 31/136 fits that pattern while 9% does not fit a clean count. An adjudicator may prefer to record this paper as reporting a range 9-23% for TikTok. Confidence set low for that reason alone; the construct itself is unambiguous (explicit misinformation coding against clinical guidelines, reported as a share of items). Note the numerator counts only videos with a HIGH amount of guideline-discordant content (>3 on the scale), so videos with 'very little' or 'moderate' misinformation are in the denominator but not the numerator - this makes the estimate conservative relative to an 'any misinformation' definition. Table 2's parenthetical view counts (34,751) are a reach/views figure, not a share, and cannot be converted to an exposure estimate because total views of all videos are not reported (only mean views per video, 43,596).

missed_or_uncertain: (1) PEMAT actionability (<75%: TikTok 87.5%, YouTube 60%) and PEMAT understandability (<75%: TikTok 38.2%, YouTube 26.7%) were deliberately NOT entered as rows: PEMAT measures whether a consumer can understand and act on the material, which is even further from veracity than DISCERN - a wholly accurate video fails it for lacking actionable steps or clear illustrations. They would be QUALITY rows if the adjudicator wants them, and the values are the ones just listed (all exact fractions of 136 and 75). (2) Commercial bias (TikTok 9.6%/9.5%, YouTube 18.6%/17%) is a conflict-of-interest measure, not misinformation or information quality - no row; note the paper also contradicts itself here (Table 2 9.6% vs text 9.5% for TikTok; 18.6% vs 17% for YouTube). (3) Component DISCERN items reported as shares (clear sources: TikTok 0%, YouTube 14.6%; areas of uncertainty: 4.5% / 12.0%; risks of treatment: 0.6% / 1.3%; actionable steps: 16.1% / 44.0%; clear illustrations: 16.8% / 42.6%) are quality sub-items, not veracity - no rows. (4) NO exposure or reach estimate is derivable: Table 2 gives view counts for poorly-scoring videos (e.g. 34,751 views for high-misinformation TikTok videos) but total views across all videos are never reported (only mean views per video: TikTok 43,596, YouTube 38,747), so the misinformation share of views cannot be computed without a cross-category construction. (5) Table 4 is internally inconsistent and I took no values from it: its 'TikTok' block sums to 132 for actionability and 90 for DISCERN, its 'YouTube' block to 90 and 119, whereas the samples are 136 and 75 - the platform labels and/or the DISCERN counts appear to be scrambled. (6) Demographic tables (Table 1: speaker gender, race, profession) are not misinformation measures. (7) Background prevalence of the CONDITION (16% of men, 17% of women affected by OAB) is cited from other papers - excluded by R8. (8) The Editorial Commentary appended to the article is a different author (Sutherland) and contains no estimates. (9) QUOTE PROVENANCE: this PDF extracts as interleaved two-column lines, so full sentences of the running text are not contiguous in the text file. Every source_quote, moderator_quote and rob quote above is a span that IS contiguous in the file; the longer definitions reproduced in the misinfo_def fields (the 5-point misinformation scale, the DISCERN poor-quality rule) are the paper's exact wording reassembled across those column breaks, with no wording changed. In the source file the scale's '=' signs render as '¼' and the '>' in Table 2's 'High misinformation (score >3)' row renders as a control character.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis at a single time point. TikTok API searched 13 February 2022 for the last 500 videos carrying #overactivebladder; YouTube searched the same day for the first 120 results for 'overactive bladder'; after excluding off-topic, non-English, over-10-minute, text-and-audio-free and provider-only surgical-technique videos, 136 TikTok and 75 YouTube videos were analysed. Both frames are rank/recency-truncated and English-only, and the authors state the sample is 'only a small proportion of the vast, and ever growing, pool of OAB content'. Videos were scored by trained reviewers after the team reached consensus ratings on 6 YouTube and 6 TikTok videos, using PEMAT (8 of 13 understandability items plus all 4 actionability items), DISCERN (poor quality <3), a published 5-point misinformation scale referenced to clinical guidelines, and a commercial-bias flag; speaker demographics were rater-assumed. No inter-rater reliability was computed for this study - 99.6% agreement between 2 coders is cited from a prior study using the same instruments - and the authors acknowledge the instruments' subjectivity. Comparisons by Mann-Whitney and chi-square in R; study deemed IRB-exempt; no funding; one author recused from editorial handling.
